title: Laboratory bleeding measures
covers: Which test probes which phase of hemostasis: platelet count and smear, PFA-100, PT, aPTT, thrombin time and fibrinogen, the PT/aPTT grid, mixing studies, factor assays, the VWF panel and pre-analytical errors.

items.p: Every lab test probes one of the three phases of hemostasis.

table: Platelet count and smear, PFA-100/200, VWF panel
PT, aPTT, thrombin time, fibrinogen, mixing study, factor assays

items.p: A platelet count of 20,000/µL disrupts primary hemostasis.

ul: Typical adult range 150–450 × 10⁹/L: below 150 = thrombocytopenia, above 450 = thrombocytosis
Usually the first screen in a bleeding workup: fast, and it excludes quantitative platelet problems
The smear asks: is the low count spurious from EDTA clumping? Are platelets giant, dysplastic or clumped? Any other CBC clue (anemia, leukocytosis, pancytopenia)?

items.p: Reduced platelet function (uremia, aspirin) adds bleeding risk at every count. A normal count with abnormal bleeding should raise suspicion of a functional platelet defect or VWD.

ul: Citrated blood is drawn through a collagen-coated membrane under high shear; the closure time is measured
Cartridges: collagen/epinephrine and collagen/ADP. It simulates adhesion, activation and aggregation.
Prolonged closure time: VWD, aspirin/NSAID effect, significant inherited platelet dysfunction
Limits: a normal PFA does not exclude mild VWD or mild platelet defects. Low hematocrit, low platelet count and pre-analytical problems prolong it.

items.p: Abnormal PFA + normal count → platelet function or VWF problem → next test: VWF panel.

table: Extrinsic + common pathway; isolated prolongation = factor VII; reported as the INR (warfarin)
Primary hemostasis (platelets, VWD) or a vascular cause
Hemophilia A or B, factor XI or XII deficiency, lupus anticoagulant
Factor VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency
Liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency or higher-dose warfarin; isolated X, II or V deficiency

ul: Infant boy bleeding after a heel stick, isolated long aPTT, normal platelets → hemophilia A or B (XII → XI → VIII/IX → X)
Warfarin, isolated long PT → extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and the INR
Decompensated cirrhosis oozing from IV sites, both prolonged → liver disease (a global process)

items.p: Patient plasma + normal plasma 1:1, then re-test.

table: Normal plasma supplied the missing factor → factor deficiency
Something in the patient's plasma also blocks the normal plasma → inhibitor (lupus anticoagulant, factor antibody)

items.p: Ordered after an isolated prolonged aPTT and a mixing study that corrects. They show which factor (VIII, IX, XI, XII) and how severe.

summary.h: The bleeding workup and the VWF panel

items.p: Bleeding history → platelet count → PT + aPTT → PFA-100 → VWF panel.

Opening case: a 19-year-old with nosebleeds since childhood, easy bruising and heavy periods (mucocutaneous, immediate). The first test is the platelet count and smear. Platelets 260,000/µL, PT 12.5 s and aPTT 34 s were normal; the PFA-100 closure time was markedly prolonged → VWF panel. A normal count and normal PT/aPTT do not rule out VWD.

ul: Type 1: partial quantitative deficiency, most common (~75%)
EDTA tube used instead of citrate
Sample left 6 hours at room temperature before testing

items.note: The slides ask which tests are distorted and in which direction but give no answer. Standard laboratory practice (not from the slides): an underfilled citrate tube has too much citrate for the plasma and falsely prolongs the PT and aPTT; an EDTA sample is rejected for clotting tests; a long delay at room temperature lets labile factors (mainly factor VIII) decay and can falsely prolong the aPTT. Only the underfilled tube is tested.

cards.q: Which phase does each test probe?
cards.a: Platelet count, smear, PFA-100, VWF panel: primary. PT, aPTT, thrombin time, fibrinogen: secondary.

cards.q: Adult platelet range and cut-offs
cards.a: 150–450 × 10⁹/L; below 150 thrombocytopenia, above 450 thrombocytosis

cards.q: Bleeding risk by platelet count
cards.a: ≥ 50,000 minimal; 20,000–50,000 minor bleeding after trauma; < 20,000 spontaneous; < 5,000 severe, possibly life-threatening

cards.q: What adds bleeding risk at any platelet count?
cards.a: Reduced platelet function (uremia, aspirin)

cards.q: Why is the CBC and smear the first test in a bleeding workup?
cards.a: Fast, and it excludes quantitative platelet problems

cards.q: Low count in a well patient with clumps on the smear?
cards.a: Spurious count from EDTA clumping

cards.q: Normal platelet count but abnormal bleeding: think of?
cards.a: A functional platelet defect or VWD

cards.q: PFA-100: how it works
cards.a: Citrated blood through a collagen-coated membrane (collagen/epinephrine, collagen/ADP) under high shear; closure time measured

cards.q: PFA-100: causes of a prolonged closure time
cards.a: VWD, aspirin/NSAID, significant inherited platelet dysfunction; also low hematocrit, low count, pre-analytical problems

cards.q: PFA-100: main limit
cards.a: A normal result does not exclude mild VWD or mild platelet defects

cards.q: Abnormal PFA-100 with a normal count: next test?
cards.a: VWF panel (VWF antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity, factor VIII activity)

cards.q: PT versus aPTT versus thrombin time
cards.a: PT: extrinsic + common. aPTT: intrinsic + common. TT: fibrinogen → fibrin.

cards.q: PT normal, aPTT prolonged: causes
cards.a: Hemophilia A or B, factor XI or XII deficiency, lupus anticoagulant

cards.q: PT prolonged, aPTT normal: causes
cards.a: Factor VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency

cards.q: PT and aPTT both prolonged: causes
cards.a: Liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency or higher-dose warfarin; isolated X, II or V deficiency

cards.q: PT and aPTT both normal but bleeding: think of?
cards.a: Primary hemostasis (platelets, VWD) or a vascular cause

cards.q: Mixing study: method and reading
cards.a: Patient + normal plasma 1:1, re-test. Corrects = factor deficiency; no correction = inhibitor (lupus anticoagulant, factor antibody)

cards.q: When is a factor assay ordered?
cards.a: After an isolated prolonged aPTT and a mixing study that corrects; it shows which factor and how severe

cards.q: Factor activity and severity
cards.a: Severe < 1%, moderate 1–5%, mild 5–40%

cards.q: Order of the bleeding workup
cards.a: Bleeding history → platelet count → PT + aPTT → PFA-100 → VWF panel

cards.q: VWF panel: the three tests
cards.a: VWF antigen (amount), ristocetin cofactor activity (function), factor VIII activity (VWF stabilizes it)

cards.q: VWD types
cards.a: Type 1 partial quantitative (~75%); type 2 qualitative; type 3 near-total, rare

cards.q: Three pre-analytical errors in coagulation testing
cards.a: EDTA tube instead of citrate; half-filled citrate tube; 6 hours at room temperature before testing

questions.stem: A 30-year-old has a platelet count of 20,000/µL with a normal PT and aPTT. Which phase of hemostasis is most directly disrupted?
questions.explanation: Platelets form the first plug, so a low count disrupts primary hemostasis. Every laboratory test probes one phase: primary, secondary or fibrinolysis. B: Secondary hemostasis; the PT and aPTT are normal. C: Clot breakdown, not plug formation. D: Not what the count reflects. E: The factor XIII step of the fibrin clot.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old on warfarin has a prolonged PT, a normal aPTT and a normal platelet count. Which pathways does the abnormal test measure?
questions.explanation: The PT measures the extrinsic and common pathways. An isolated prolonged PT points to the extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and is reported as the INR. A: The aPTT (intrinsic), which is normal. B: The PFA-100. C: Not measured by the PT. E: The thrombin time.

questions.stem: Which test measures the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin?
questions.explanation: Four basic tests: PT (extrinsic + common), aPTT (intrinsic + common), thrombin time (common pathway, fibrinogen → fibrin), fibrinogen concentration (substrate for clot formation). A: Extrinsic and common pathways. B: Intrinsic and common pathways. D: Platelet function. E: One intrinsic factor.

questions.stem: An adult's platelet count is 480 × 10⁹/L. How is this classified?
questions.explanation: Typical adult range 150–450 × 10⁹/L: below 150 = thrombocytopenia, above 450 = thrombocytosis. A: The upper limit is 450 × 10⁹/L. B: Clumping lowers the count. C: A count says nothing about function. D: Lowers the count.

questions.stem: A healthy 40-year-old with no bleeding history has a platelet count of 45 × 10⁹/L on an EDTA sample. The smear shows large platelet clumps. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: The smear checks whether the count is spurious because of EDTA clumping, and whether platelets are giant, dysplastic or clumped. A: Clumps on the smear explain the low count. C: No other cytopenia and no bleeding. D: No splenomegaly; clumps explain it. E: Clumps are not giant single platelets.

questions.stem: Why is the CBC with smear usually the first test in a bleeding workup?

options.A: It quickly excludes a platelet number problem
options.B: It measures platelet adhesion under shear
options.C: It detects mild von Willebrand disease

questions.explanation: The CBC + smear is usually the first screen in a bleeding workup because it is fast and helps exclude quantitative platelet problems. B: The PFA-100. C: Needs the VWF panel. D: The PT. E: The mixing study.

questions.stem: A man has a platelet count of 35,000/µL. What bleeding is expected at this count?
questions.explanation: Bleeding risk: ≥ 50,000/µL minimal; 20,000–50,000/µL minor bleeding after trauma; < 20,000/µL spontaneous bleeding; < 5,000/µL severe, possibly life-threatening spontaneous bleeding. A: At or above 50,000/µL. B: Below 20,000/µL. C: Below 5,000/µL. E: A clotting factor pattern.

questions.stem: Below which platelet count does spontaneous bleeding become expected?
questions.explanation: Below 20,000/µL: spontaneous bleeding; below 5,000/µL: severe, possibly life-threatening spontaneous bleeding. A: Below this, bleeding after trauma. B: Minimal risk. D: The lower limit of normal. E: Severe, possibly life-threatening bleeding.

questions.stem: A child has a platelet count of 4,000/µL. Which bleeding risk does this carry?
questions.explanation: Below 5,000/µL the risk is severe, possibly life-threatening spontaneous bleeding. A: 20,000–50,000/µL. B: ≥ 50,000/µL. C: Understates the risk. D: A clotting factor pattern.

questions.stem: Two patients have platelet counts of 30,000/µL. One has end-stage renal disease and bleeds more. What explains the difference?
questions.explanation: Reduced platelet function (e.g. due to uremia or aspirin use) adds risk of bleeding in each platelet count range. A: Not the uremic effect. C: Not the explanation given. D: The counts are equal. E: Would not increase bleeding.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has lifelong nosebleeds and gum bleeding. Her platelet count, PT and aPTT are normal. Which disorder is most likely?
questions.explanation: A normal count with abnormal (lifelong mucocutaneous) bleeding should raise suspicion of a functional platelet defect or VWD. A: Male, joint and deep bleeding, prolonged aPTT. B: Prolonged PT. C: Low count. E: Prolonged PT.

questions.stem: What does the PFA-100 closure time assess?
questions.explanation: PFA-100/200 screens platelet adhesion/aggregation function under high shear: not the number, the function. A: The platelet count. B: The thrombin time. C: A factor assay. D: Fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: PFA-100 cartridges pair epinephrine or ADP with which substance?
questions.explanation: Citrated blood is drawn through a collagen-coated membrane under high shear (collagen/epinephrine and collagen/ADP cartridges), and closure time is measured. A: The PT trigger. C: The thrombin time reagent. D: The substrate, not the coating. E: Used in VWF activity testing.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old taking daily aspirin has a normal platelet count, PT and aPTT. Which result is most likely abnormal?
questions.explanation: A prolonged closure time supports a platelet-type problem: VWD, aspirin/NSAID effect, or significant inherited platelet dysfunction. B: Fibrinogen to fibrin. C: Not affected by aspirin. D: Not affected by aspirin. E: No prolonged clotting time to mix.

questions.stem: A boy with mild mucocutaneous bleeding has a normal PFA-100 closure time. Which condition is still possible?
questions.explanation: Important limits: a normal PFA does not exclude mild VWD or mild platelet defects. Low hematocrit, low platelet count and pre-analytical issues can prolong it. A: Severe; would prolong closure time. B: Significant inherited dysfunction prolongs it. D: A low count prolongs it. E: A low hematocrit prolongs it.

questions.stem: A woman with a hematocrit of 18% has a normal platelet count, takes no drugs and has a normal VWF panel. Her PFA-100 closure time is prolonged. What best explains it?
questions.explanation: Low hematocrit, low platelet count and pre-analytical issues can prolong the PFA closure time. A: The PFA does not test factors. C: The PFA does not test factors. D: Affects the aPTT. E: Not a cause.

questions.stem: A patient has an abnormal PFA-100 and a normal platelet count. What does this suggest?

options.D: A defect of the vessel wall
options.E: A platelet function or VWF problem

questions.explanation: The PFA-100 screens function, not quantity. With a normal count, an abnormal result points to a platelet function or VWF-related problem; the next test is the VWF panel. A: The count is normal. B: The PFA does not test factors. C: Not tested by the PFA. D: Not tested by the PFA.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has had nosebleeds since childhood, easy bruising and heavy menstrual bleeding. The exam is otherwise normal. What is the best first laboratory test?
questions.explanation: Bleeding history → platelet count/smear → PT + aPTT → PFA-100 → VWF panel. The count and smear is the right first move. A: Come after the count. B: Comes after the PFA-100. D: Not the first move. E: Not a first test.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding. Platelets are 260,000/µL, PT 12.5 s and aPTT 34 s. The PFA-100 closure time is markedly prolonged. What is the next test?
questions.explanation: A normal platelet count and normal PT/aPTT did not rule out VWD: the abnormal PFA-100 led to the VWF panel (VWF antigen, VWF activity/ristocetin cofactor, factor VIII activity). A: aPTT normal; mucocutaneous pattern. B: Nothing prolonged to mix. C: The count is normal. E: Fibrinogen to fibrin.

questions.stem: In what order is a bleeding workup built?
questions.explanation: Algorithm: bleeding history → platelet count → PT + aPTT → PFA-100 → VWF panel. B: History comes first. C: History and count come first. D: The count precedes the PFA. E: History comes first.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy has prolonged bleeding after a heel stick. The PT is normal, the aPTT prolonged and the platelet count normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Isolated prolonged aPTT → intrinsic pathway factors (XII → XI → VIII/IX → X): hemophilia A (VIII) or B (IX). A: Prolongs the PT. C: Prolongs the PT too. D: Prolongs the PT first. E: Normal aPTT.

questions.stem: An infant's isolated prolonged aPTT corrects on 1:1 mixing with normal plasma. Which test identifies the missing factor and its severity?
questions.explanation: Factor assays are ordered after an isolated prolonged aPTT and a mixing study that corrects: they pinpoint which factor (VIII, IX, XI, XII) and how severe. A: How much VWF is present. B: Platelet function. C: Fibrinogen to fibrin. E: Already shows a deficiency.

questions.stem: A boy's factor VIII activity is 0.6%. How is his deficiency graded?
questions.explanation: Factor activity level determines severity: severe < 1%, moderate 1–5%, mild 5–40%. B: 1–5%. C: 5–40%. D: Not a severity grade. E: Not a severity grade.

questions.stem: A boy's factor IX activity is 3%. How is his deficiency graded?
questions.explanation: Severe < 1%, moderate 1–5%, mild 5–40%. A: < 1%. B: 5–40%. D: Not a severity grade. E: Not a severity grade.

questions.stem: Each prolongs the aPTT with a normal PT EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: PT normal + aPTT prolonged: hemophilia A/B, factor XI or XII deficiency, lupus anticoagulant. Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT alone. A: Intrinsic factor. B: Intrinsic factor. C: Isolated prolonged aPTT. D: Factor IX, intrinsic.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has a prolonged aPTT and a normal PT. The aPTT stays prolonged after 1:1 mixing with normal plasma. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: No correction on mixing = an inhibitor in the patient's plasma (e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor antibody). B: Would correct on mixing. C: Would correct on mixing. D: Prolongs the PT. E: Prolongs the PT.

questions.stem: A prolonged aPTT corrects after 1:1 mixing with normal plasma. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: Corrects: normal plasma supplied the missing factor → the patient is missing a clotting factor. A: Would not correct. B: Does not affect the aPTT. C: Not tested by mixing. E: Affects the PFA, not mixing.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has new large bruises. His aPTT is prolonged with a normal PT and does not correct after 1:1 mixing. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Does not correct: something in the patient's plasma actively blocks normal plasma too → an inhibitor (e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor antibody). A: Would correct. B: Would correct. D: Prolongs the PT. E: Prolongs the PT.

questions.stem: In a mixing study, patient plasma is mixed with normal plasma in what ratio before re-testing?
questions.explanation: Patient plasma + normal plasma, 1:1, then re-test. A: Not the ratio. C: Not the ratio. D: The citrate-to-blood ratio of the tube. E: Not the ratio.

questions.stem: Why does a mixing study fail to correct when an inhibitor is present?

options.A: Normal plasma lacks the missing factor
options.B: The inhibitor destroys platelets in the tube
options.E: The inhibitor also blocks the normal plasma

questions.explanation: Does not correct: something in the patient's plasma is actively blocking normal plasma too → an inhibitor is present. A: It supplies it. B: Plasma test; no platelets. C: Not the reason. D: Not the reason.

questions.stem: An isolated prolonged PT in a patient on warfarin reflects a fall in which factor?
questions.explanation: Isolated prolonged PT → think extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and the INR. A: Intrinsic; aPTT. B: Intrinsic; aPTT. D: Intrinsic; aPTT. E: Intrinsic; aPTT.

questions.stem: Which value derived from the PT is used to monitor warfarin?
questions.explanation: Isolated prolonged PT → think extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and the INR. A: The intrinsic test. B: Fibrinogen to fibrin. C: Platelet function. D: Fibrin breakdown.

questions.stem: A patient on long-term antibiotics with poor intake has a prolonged PT and a normal aPTT. If the cause is not corrected, which change follows?
questions.explanation: Early vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT alone (factor VII); more severe vitamin K deficiency prolongs both PT and aPTT. A: Not a vitamin K effect. C: Fibrinogen is not vitamin K dependent. D: Platelet function. E: Not vitamin K dependent.

questions.stem: A patient with decompensated cirrhosis oozes from IV sites. PT and aPTT are prolonged and platelets are low-normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Both prolonged → think common pathway or a global process (liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency). B: The aPTT would be normal. C: The PT would be normal. D: Normal PT and aPTT. E: Isolated aPTT.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old with lifelong bleeding has a prolonged PT and aPTT that correct on mixing. Liver tests and fibrinogen are normal and he takes no drugs. Which single deficiency fits?
questions.explanation: Prolonged PT with prolonged PTT: combined deficiencies (liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency) or isolated deficiencies of factor X, II or V. A: PT alone. B: aPTT alone. C: aPTT alone. E: Both normal.

questions.stem: Each prolongs both the PT and the aPTT EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Early warfarin effect prolongs the PT alone (with factor VII deficiency and early vitamin K deficiency). Both prolonged: liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency/warfarin (higher dose), factor X, II or V deficiency. A: Global process. C: Global process. D: Common pathway. E: Common pathway.

questions.stem: A septic patient oozes from IV lines. PT and aPTT are prolonged and the platelet count is low. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Both prolonged → a global process such as liver disease, DIC or vitamin K deficiency; the low count fits DIC. A: PT and aPTT normal. B: Thrombosis; not this picture. C: PT alone; count normal. D: Normal PT and aPTT.

questions.stem: An elderly woman has flat purple patches on her forearms. Platelet count, PT and aPTT are normal. Where is the problem most likely?
questions.explanation: Both normal: consider primary hemostasis (platelets, VWD) or a vascular cause. B: PT normal. C: aPTT normal. D: Both normal. E: Both normal.

questions.stem: A patient has a prolonged PT and aPTT. Which result points to a fibrinogen problem rather than a factor X deficiency?
questions.explanation: The thrombin time tests the last step (fibrinogen → fibrin); fibrinogen concentration is the substrate. Factor X acts before thrombin, so the thrombin time stays normal in factor X deficiency. A: Platelet function. B: Not specific. C: Both are deficiencies. E: Unrelated.

questions.stem: Which VWF panel test measures how well VWF functions?
questions.explanation: VWF panel: VWF antigen (how much), VWF activity/ristocetin cofactor (how well it functions), factor VIII activity (VWF stabilizes factor VIII). A: How much VWF is present. B: The carried factor. D: Not part of the panel. E: Not part of the panel.

questions.stem: Why does a VWF panel include factor VIII activity?

options.D: VWF is made from factor VIII

questions.explanation: The panel measures VWF antigen, VWF activity (ristocetin cofactor) and factor VIII activity, because VWF stabilizes factor VIII. A: Reversed. C: ADAMTS-13 does. D: Separate proteins. E: VWF binds GPIb.

questions.stem: A woman with heavy periods has VWF antigen and VWF activity both mildly and proportionally reduced. Which type of von Willebrand disease is most likely?
questions.explanation: Type 1: partial quantitative deficiency, the most common (~75%). B: Function low out of proportion to antigen. C: Near-total deficiency. D: Not suggested. E: Not a VWD type.

questions.stem: A man's VWF antigen is normal, but his ristocetin cofactor activity is markedly reduced. Which type of von Willebrand disease is most likely?
questions.explanation: Type 2: a qualitative/functional defect (several subtypes): VWF is present but works poorly. A: Antigen and function fall together. B: Antigen near-absent. C: Not suggested. E: Not a VWD type.

questions.stem: A child with severe bleeding has nearly undetectable VWF antigen and activity and a very low factor VIII. Which type of von Willebrand disease is this?
questions.explanation: Type 3: severe, near-total deficiency, rare. Factor VIII is low because VWF stabilizes it. A: Partial deficiency. B: Qualitative defect. D: Not suggested. E: Not a VWD type.

questions.stem: About what share of von Willebrand disease is type 1?
questions.explanation: Type 1 is the most common (~75%). A: Too low. B: Too low. C: Too high. D: Too low.

questions.stem: A citrate tube for coagulation tests is only half-filled with blood. What is the expected effect?
questions.explanation: The slides pose this without an answer; standard laboratory practice: an underfilled tube has excess citrate for the plasma volume, which binds the calcium added in the test, so clotting times are falsely prolonged. A: A count is not run on this tube. B: Not the effect. C: Not the effect. E: The ratio matters.

questions.stem: Each is a pre-analytical error that can distort coagulation results EXCEPT:

options.A: A lupus anticoagulant in the sample
options.B: An EDTA tube used instead of citrate
options.D: Six hours at room temperature before testing

questions.explanation: Pre-analytical errors silently distort coagulation results: tube switch (EDTA instead of citrate), underfilled citrate tube, delayed transport (6 hours at room temperature). A lupus anticoagulant is a true patient inhibitor, not a sampling error. B: Wrong tube. C: Wrong ratio. D: Delayed transport. E: Factors consumed in the tube.
